FLORIDA JUST TOOK A MAJOR STEP TOWARD ELIMINATING PROPERTY TAXES — IS THIS THE BEGINNING OF A MUCH BIGGER TRANSITION? 🇺🇸

On November 3, 2026, Florida voters APPROVED Amendment 3, fundamentally restructuring how property taxes are assessed on primary residences.

LOOK AT WHAT JUST HAPPENED:

🇺🇸 Homestead exemption increases to $150,000 in 2027.

🇺🇸 Exemption increases again to $250,000 in 2028.

🇺🇸 Inflation adjustments begin in 2029.

🇺🇸 Annual assessment increases on non-homestead properties are capped at 5%, down from 10%, excluding school taxes.

🇺🇸 Millions of Florida homeowners could see substantial reductions in their property-tax obligations.

NOW CONSIDER THE BIGGER PICTURE.

For years, we’ve been examining the THEORY that President Trump’s long-term economic agenda involves fundamentally restructuring America’s financial and taxation systems.

That includes the possibility of eventually reducing reliance on federal income taxes and local property taxes in favor of alternative revenue models.

We’ve also discussed the THEORY that Florida has served as a model state for broader reforms involving individual freedom, economic independence, sovereignty and government accountability.

WHAT IF FLORIDA IS BECOMING A REAL-WORLD TEST CASE?

Think about the potential sequence:

1. Establish a state with no individual income tax.
2. Dramatically reduce property taxes on primary residences.
3. Force a reassessment of local government spending and revenue.
4. Demonstrate whether the new system can sustain essential services.
5. Provide a potential blueprint for other states to evaluate.

Florida already had no state individual income tax. Now its voters have approved a major constitutional reduction in property taxation.

IS THIS PART OF A BROADER ECONOMIC TRANSITION? 

I believe so.

Within our ongoing interpretation of Trump’s long-term agenda, the timing is certainly worth examining.

Florida has taken a significant step toward reducing one of the largest recurring tax obligations associated with homeownership.

And if other states begin considering similar reforms, we may be witnessing the emergence of a much larger national policy trend.

Sometimes the most important developments aren’t just about what happened today.

They’re about what those developments could make possible tomorrow.

The American people have spoken. America must come to terms with how much its electorate has changed and what that could mean for future elections.

One factor I believe is often overlooked is bloc voting. In Michigan, Muslim voters may rally behind a Muslim candidate they see as a voice for their community. In Minnesota, Somali American voters may do the same for a Somali American candidate. In a close race, that kind of support can make the difference.

Now look at what happened in three states Republicans counted on.

Greg Abbott’s top donor was a Pakistani Muslim.

Texas has the fastest-growing Muslim population in America and the largest number of new mosques.

He thought he could appease Muslims and win their votes. In the end, they voted him out.

In Florida, Republicans held on to both offices, but the margins were slim. Byron Donalds narrowly defeated David Jolly in the governor’s race, and Ashley Moody held the U.S. Senate seat by about three percentage points over Angie Nixon. Just four years ago, Ron DeSantis won reelection by nearly 20 points.

And in South Carolina, what was supposed to be a stroll in the park for Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, turned into a bitter defeat. Democrat Annie Andrews flipped the Senate seat. In my view, Graham was the wrong candidate for the job and ran a terrible campaign.

Republicans have a lot of soul-searching to do.

One thing I’m sure of is that the woke right will blame these losses on the war with Iran and, from there, find a way to make it Israel’s fault. What can I say? If we can get blamed for a train crash in Spain, I suppose we can take this one too.

The 2026 midterms may be just the appetizer. The main course is the 2028 presidential election. If the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) consolidate their influence and more of their allies move into key positions, they will have a greater say in whom the party nominates and what policies it pursues. Americans should insist on transparency and accountability at every stage of the election process.

Sadly, I believe the next swing of the pendulum could be more turbulent. If Americans see socialism, Islamist extremism, and antisemitism gaining ground in their country, how long can we expect the silent majority to stay silent?

For believers, I pray that the coming years will be a wake-up call to return to God, stand firmly on His Word, and hold fast to sound doctrine.

The days are evil, and we must redeem the time! (Ephesians 5:16)
